extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and formal-methods contributors (potential Flyspeck participants) interested in formalizing the Kepler Conjecture
extracted.subtask_short: formalizing Kepler conjecture in HOL Light
extracted.subtask_description: Produce a machine-checked formal proof of the Kepler Conjecture by encoding and checking the full proof in HOL Light (with possible contributions from Coq/Isabelle), implemented in Objective CAML. The page summarizes goals, tools, rationale, and resources for participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal-proof completeness (supply all intermediate logical steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a formal proof, all the intermediate logical steps are supplied. No appeal is made to intuition, even if the translation from intuition to logic is routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts traditional mathematical proofs (which omit routine logical steps and assume context) with formal proofs which include every intermediate step so they are less intuitive but less susceptible to logical errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-checked proofs (use of theorem provers)
rubrics_metrics.description: All the formal proofs will be made by computer and programmed in the Objective CAML programming language. The steps of the proof will be generated by computer programs using John Harrison's HOL light software package, with contributions from other systems such as Coq and Isabelle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a requirement for the project: proofs must be produced by computer tooling (HOL Light primary, Coq/Isabelle possible), not as informal human-only derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool choice: Objective CAML (OCaml) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective CAML was selected for this project because HOL light is written in this language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: contributors should learn/use OCaml; resources and tutorials on OCaml are provided/linked on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design source: base on 1998 Hales–Ferguson proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The design of the proof will be based on the 1998 (traditional-style) proof of the Kepler Conjecture by Hales and Ferguson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formalization is not a novel independent proof but a machine-checked encoding of the established 1998 proof; contributors should work from those tex/source files (linked under the project's source tab).

rubrics_metrics.name: HOL Light reliability criteria (small kernel, type checking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system is built on a small kernel, and the type checking insures that no fatal bugs can occur outside the kernel. That is, if you leave a bug in your code, the worst that can happen is that you will fail to prove a theorem you hoped to prove. You can never put a bug in your code that yields a false statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph is used to justify selection of HOL Light: small trusted base and strong type guarantees reduce the risk that the prover produces false theorems. It is an explicit quality criterion for the proof infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: HOL Light proof-construct validity (theorem data type guarantee)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the system there is a 'theorem' data type. Each value of this type is the statement of a mathematical theorem. The type checking system in Objective CAML prevents the creation of a value of this type, except by rules that insure that the statement has a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guarantee: a produced value of type 'theorem' (e.g., expressing 'The Kepler Conjecture is true') means the system has checked every logical step in the derivation; this is the formal certification goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on opaque algorithms (transparency over closed-source numeric routines)
rubrics_metrics.description: How does HOL light differ from packages such as Mathematica? In Mathematica, procedures may rely on algorithms of unknown origin and unknown reliability; in HOL Light, by the time it returns a theorem the computer has checked every logical step in the derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes a criterion: prefer systems and procedures where each step is verifiable rather than relying on black-box numeric routines whose correctness cannot be certified within the proof assistant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintainability & inspectability of prover code
rubrics_metrics.description: The source code is short and quite readable. Thus, any questions about the behavior of the system can be resolved through the syntax and semantics of the underlying language (Objective CAML).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of HOL Light is justified by its readable, concise source that makes auditing the trusted code base feasible; contributors should expect to be able to inspect system behavior through its source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-checking behavior (HOL Light becomes self-checking after base code)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system becomes self-checking after the first thousand lines of code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: once the core is in place, the system's subsequent developments rely on the formal kernel to enforce correctness; trust is primarily in the small kernel and its initial correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project goal: produce a HOL Light 'theorem' for Kepler Conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the flyspeck project is to produce a value of type 'theorem' in HOL light that expresses the statement 'The Kepler Conjecture is true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the explicit deliverable/acceptance criterion for the project: a machine-checkable theorem object representing the Kepler Conjecture in HOL Light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope/scale expectation (project size)
rubrics_metrics.description: How large a project is the flyspeck project? The project has about 500,000 lines of code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical expectation for contributors: the formalization is large-scale, implying substantial effort, coordination, and familiarity with large codebases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff: formal proofs are less intuitive but more reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus, a formal proof is less intuitive, and yet less susceptible to logical errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes an evaluative tradeoff contributors should accept: decreased human-level readability/intuitiveness in exchange for mechanical certainty and error resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite resources and background (tools and mathematical texts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The page lists resources: OCaml tutorials, HOL Light manual, introductions to the Kepler Conjecture, tex files for the proof, and books giving geometry background (recommended textbooks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: contributors are expected to consult these resources to acquire necessary programming and mathematical background before contributing; specific recommended readings are named (Euclidean and non-euclidean geometry by Patrick Ryan; Euclidean Geometry and Convexity by Russell Benson; algorithmic/computational geometry texts).
